content.title: Eid-ul-Fitr 2026: When will Eid be celebrated in India, March 20 or 21? Check date, Chand Raat, significan
content.text: Middle East tensions have pushed geopolitics back into the centre of market pricing, reviving an old vulnerability for energy-importing economies across Asia. For Indian investors, the concern is not limited to a single headline or one trading session. The immediate issue is a familiar one: an oil shock through the Strait of Hormuz would mean higher freight costs. What complicates this today is speed: information now spreads so quickly that it can shift risk appetite and investor positioning even before markets have time to thoroughly assess the disruption’s implications for growth and inflation.That combination has been visible in the way volatility has repriced. India VIX, a widely tracked gauge of near-term market fear, moved up sharply as the risk-off tone intensified. After closing at 17.13 on March 2, it rose to over 21 on March 4, as investors paid up for protection amid heightened uncertainty. Asia’s selloff deepens amid rising oil risesAcross the region, the selloff has been swift and broad-based. In a notable drop, South Korea’s KOSPI dropped more than 12%, in what was reported to be its worst-ever crash, triggering a trading halt. Japan’s Nikkei fell to 3.5%, and Taiwan’s benchmark also slid sharply as investors cut risk, with a surge in semiconductor selling.Oil has been the market’s primary transmission channel. Brent crude has traded in the low-to-mid $80s range as of March 4, extending gains since the conflict began and keeping investors focused on the risk that disruptions in the Gulf could translate into higher inflation and delayed rate cuts globally. In London, the risk premium showed up not just in equities but in the broader macro narrative. The investors were increasingly worried that a sustained rise in oil and gas prices could complicate the disinflation path and reduce central banks’ room to ease policy as quickly as markets had hoped. Why the Strait of Hormuz matters for IndiaAt the heart of the anxiety is the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow shipping route that has outsized importance for global energy flows. The US Energy Information Administration estimates that about 20 million barrels per day of petroleum liquids moved through Hormuz in 2024, accounting for roughly 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption, with these flows holding steady near these levels into 2025. For India, the risk is not only price but continuity. India’s crude import dependence remains high, cited to be around the high-80s per cent range, as per data released by Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) for FY25, which means a sharp move in oil can feed into the rupee, inflation expectations, and corporate margins faster than many other economies. Even if a full-scale disruption does not materialise, markets tend to price the tail risk early, through higher insurance costs, rerouting, longer delivery times, and precautionary inventory behaviour. Those costs can quietly seep into inflation and profitability, and they can create second-order effects in sectors such as aviation, logistics, chemicals, and consumer-facing businesses.The risk that worries policy makers: “Higher for longer” inflation in the WestA prolonged conflict could also potentially complicate the global inflation outlook at a sensitive time. While oil has not yet hit $100, some analysts draw scenarioswhere an extended blockage or deeper disruption could push prices into the high-$90s or above, depending on duration and severity. That matters because the US and Europe are still managing sticky inflation dynamics. A renewed energy impulse can keep headline inflation elevated, harden inflation expectations, and delay the pivot to lower rates. In market terms, it can shift the debate from “how limited will cuts be” to “will the rising inflation hamper rate-cuts”, which typically tightens financial conditions.India’s unique balancing actFor India, the challenge is multi-layered.First, energy sovereignty. India has to ensure that oil and natural gas supplies are not interrupted, and this has to become a long-term strategic priority, not just a present procurement problem. Any signal of chokepoint risk tends to show up quickly in freight rates and insurance premiums, even before physical shortages appear.Second, safeguarding the growth trajectory. Persistently high oil prices can act like a tax on households and businesses, pressuring consumption and margins. The effects often arrive unevenly across sectors, which is why index-level moves can hide churn underneath.Third, diplomacy without binary choices. India’s strategic posture has typically aimed at maintaining relationships across blocs. In an environment where supply chains, payments, and shipping routes are increasingly influenced by geopolitics, that balancing act becomes more important and more complex.What this means for investors: Avoid binary calls, build resilienceFor Indian investors, this phase calls for patience and process. In high-volatility markets, the most damaging outcomes often come from forced decisions: selling risk assets into a drawdown, then struggling to re-enter when markets stabilise.The early stages of a shock are often mechanical. Systematic strategies reduce exposure. Hedging demand rises. Liquidity thins. Volatility jumps. India VIX’s move this week is a reminder that the “price of protection” can re-rate quickly when uncertainty rises. That is also where portfolio construction matters more than prediction. A measured allocation to investment-grade fixed-income assets, such as government and corporate bonds, may offer stability to limit drawdowns during abrupt repricings, provide predictable cash flows to support planning in uncertain periods, and create scheduled maturities or inflows that allow investors to add to equities if valuations become attractive. This does not mean bonds are risk-free. Credit quality, liquidity, and interest-rate sensitivity matter, especially when inflation expectations are shifting. But for investors seeking to anchor portfolios over what could be a longer short- to medium-term period of geopolitical uncertainty, diversified, investment-grade exposure is increasingly part of the conversation.The market is asking a different question nowThe first-order move, risk-off, higher volatility, oil-led churn, is familiar. The more consequential question is what comes next: whether the conflict drags out, whether energy markets stay tight, and whether inflation in the US and Europe remains sticky enough to delay rate cuts.Until clearer signs emerge on conflict duration, energy implications, and sticky inflation in the US and Europe, investors may prioritise building resilient portfolios through diversification, such as opting for balanced equity-fixed income mixes instead of bold unidimensional bets.
